title: DSINC beyond Heston: the 3/2 and other non-affine stochastic-volatility models
abstract: This paper extends the damped-sinc (DSINC) method for American options beyond the affine Heston class to general one-factor stochastic-volatility models. We show that the collapse identity, which reduces the early-exercise integral to a single spectral integral, remains valid for these models. Damping between zero and one is admissible whenever the discounted spot is a nonnegative local martingale. An Itô transformation of the volatility factorizes the conditional characteristic function and identifies a natural coordinate for approximating the exercise boundary. The 3/2 model admits closed-form joint transforms in terms of Kummer functions, while uncorrelated SABR admits a Bessel representation. When a practical closed-form transform is unavailable, the required volatility integral is computed directly by solving one backward equation per frequency, without a grid in the log-price. Through a known change of volatility coordinate, this approach also accommodates correlated SABR. Tests on the 3/2, SABR, GARCH and lognormal-volatility models show agreement with fine finite-difference benchmarks to within one basis point of the strike. Computational cost is comparable to or lower than that of our finite-difference implementation, except for the slower Hankel implementation of uncorrelated SABR.

bite.hook: We extend the damped-sinc method for American options beyond the affine Heston class to general stochastic volatility models.
tldr: Extended the damped-sinc (DSINC) method for pricing American options to general one-factor stochastic-volatility models.
Demonstrated that the collapse identity remains valid, reducing the early-exercise integral to a single spectral integral.
Tested on 3/2, SABR, GARCH, and lognormal models, matching fine finite-difference benchmarks within one basis point.
bite.whyItMatters: Accurately pricing financial options under realistic market conditions is notoriously difficult and computationally expensive. This mathematical advance provides fast, highly accurate option pricing for a much broader family of market models.
bite.eli5: Financial options let you buy or sell stocks at a set price later. Figuring out the fair price when market volatility bounces around randomly is tricky. This paper provides a clever mathematical shortcut to calculate these prices much faster without losing accuracy.

glossary.shortDef: A modeling approach where the volatility of a stock is treated as a random process rather than a constant.
glossary.eli5Def: Treating the unpredictability of the stock market as its own rolling wave of random change.

glossary.shortDef: A financial derivative contract that can be exercised at any time before its expiration date.
glossary.eli5Def: A ticket that lets you buy or sell a stock whenever you want before a certain deadline.

glossary.shortDef: A sequence of random variables where the expected future value equals the present value.
glossary.eli5Def: A fair game where, on average, you expect neither to win nor lose money in the future.
